summary:
Bitlis province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked draft omnibus law, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. The draft would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a condition, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. It had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Kaos GL's 2025 report, launched under the title "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates how the pending draft is already being applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds that risk nationwide. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The legal argument against GBT stops rests on Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, to which Türkiye is a party, rather than on domestic statute. Visitors therefore have a treaty-based complaint available in principle, but the reporting indicates that stops are completed and individuals documented before any challenge can be made.

Enforcement figures available for this dossier come from Istanbul, the largest city and the centre of Pride activity, and from Ankara, the capital, where Sincan Women's Prison is located. Bitlis is a smaller eastern province with no documented LGBT policing data in the sources reviewed, so the national pattern is the reliable basis for expectation-setting rather than any local count.

Opposition to the draft package is organised and public: 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have registered their objection, and the Sincan death was raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025. Contestation exists at institutional level even though it has not yet altered enforcement practice.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, establishes that beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people predate the post-2018 legal changes. It is historical evidence of depth, not a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same draft package as visitors, but with consequences that outlast a border crossing: the proposed minimum age of 25 for gender-affirming care and the mandatory infertility condition would bind Turkish citizens and residents directly, as would the penalties proposed for health professionals providing that care.

Kaos GL's 2025 report functions as the principal domestic record of violations, compiled and published by a Turkish organisation whose lawyer, Kerem Dikmen, presented the findings at the launch. Domestic documentation exists and is publicly attributed.

Regulatory and supervisory bodies restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom throughout 2025 under a "Year of the Family" banner, with instructions issued to public institutions. Residents working in media, education, art and public administration operate under that supervisory climate.

Trans prisoners are assigned by registered sex, and the conditions of that placement were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025, including an opposition MP's parliamentary question of 12 December 2025 and coordinated demands for an independent investigation from Human Rights Association branches in six cities.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that preceded it govern how hospitals record and report gender-related care for residents, removing the "other" option and requiring electronic reports.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bitlis-specific source material was available in this inventory. There is no documented count of GBT stops, Pride events, detentions or hate incidents attributable to Bitlis province itself; the enforcement figures cited are Istanbul's and Ankara's.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of 29 October 2025 and had not been passed at that date. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources reviewed, and the dossier does not assert its current status.

The claim that enforcement is already being applied as though the draft prohibitions were in force rests on the account of one detained woman in Istanbul and on the pattern of GBT stops; no official statement confirming pre-legislative enforcement was located.

Whether the Health Ministry regulation of September 2025 restricts access to transition care in practice, as distinct from changing how it is recorded, is unresolved. The sources describe the risk of profiling and restricted access rather than measured outcomes.

Prison monitoring findings derive from a country-level profile and from accounts given about the Sincan case; independent investigation into that death had been demanded but no outcome is recorded in the sources reviewed.
